Assessment of sites based on known biology of specific tumor type
Staging: common language regarding a particular tumor group, generally based on disease
extent
Categories determine prognosis and direct treatment approaches.

Definitions
In general, musculoskeletal tumors are classified based on the tissue they derive from
and biologic aggressiveness. The most commonly used broad terms are benign and
malignant bone tumors and benign and malignant soft-tissue tumors. Based on the
natural history of a particular tumor type, the extent of disease is assessed via physical
examination and imaging studies. Staging is a method of communicating the extent of
disease for a tumor type or group of tumors in a manner that categorizes prognosis for
an individual patient and allows for comparisons among groups regarding outcomes.
Knowledge of necessary elements to properly stage a musculoskeletal tumor serves as a
guide to determine the extent of disease that must be assessed for in each patient
based on the classification of the tumor.


Classification
Bone tumors are classified into general categories of benign or malignant. Benign
tumors have no metastatic potential. Malignant tumors have varying metastatic
potential based on grade. Tumors that have varying biologic aggressiveness often are
categorized as atypical or of uncertain metastatic potential. Some cartilage tumors and
giant cell tumors of bone fit into this category. Whether a bone tumor is benign or
malignant often aids in classification as intramedullary or surface tumors, which aids in


Staging
This surgical staging system was helpful to surgeons as a common language after it was
published in 1980 (Resource 3). It was never favored by medical/pediatric oncologists or
radiation oncologists and was not able to adapt as other prognostic factors were
identified. Most practitioners use the tumor, nodes, and metastasis (TNM) system for
prognostic staging (Resource 2).
The T designation is based on tumor size, with an 8-cm cutoff for most sites. For spine
tumors, the T designation is based on how many segments are involved and whether the
spinal canal or great vessels are involved. For pelvic bone sarcomas, the T designation is
based on size, the amount of the pelvis involved in bone and out of bone, and whether
the tumor invades the sacrum or major vessels.
Grade is split into high and low, with a separate designation for high grade moderately
differentiated and high grade poorly differentiated. For non–spine-pelvis locations, low-
grade tumors are stage IA or stage IB based on size, T1 and T2, respectively. High-grade
tumors are stage IIA or stage IIB based on size.
The T3 designation is for skip metastases within the same bone as the primary tumor
and immediately increases the stage, indicating a poorer prognosis.
Pulmonary-only metastatic disease increases the stage to IVA, whereas any nodal
involvement or non-pulmonary metastatic disease increases the stage to IVB. This is
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:40 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002072

because pulmonary metastatic disease is associated with a better prognosis than nodal
(rare for bone sarcomas) or non-pulmonary disease extent.
Currently, this staging system is commonly used for bone sarcomas other than those in
the Ewing sarcoma family of tumors, which has differences to allow for bone marrow
involvement among other factors.
As stage increases, prognosis decreases, and treating providers are more likely to
recommend systemic therapy in addition to local control measures.

Classification
Hundreds of different soft-tissue tumors exist, most of which are classified based on the
suspected originating cell or tissue type. Molecular analysis of soft-tissue tumors is
becoming a more predominant method for classification because of better
understanding of the genetic basis of tumors and the development of therapy that can
target specific abnormalities in the driver or downstream pathways.


Malignant
The TNM staging system for soft-tissue sarcomas, which is the result of the combined
efforts of the American Joint Committee on Cancer and the Union for International
Cancer Control, includes more prognostic factors than earlier versions. Retroperitoneal
soft-tissue sarcomas are specifically staged separately because of poorer prognosis and
anatomic constraints.
For extremity/trunk tumors, the T designation is based on the size of the primary tumor,
with 5-, 10-, and 15-cm increments.
Grade is effectively low or high.
Low-grade tumors are stage IA for T1 tumors (≤5 cm) and stage IB for tumors larger than
5 cm (T2, T3, T4). High-grade tumors are stage IIA for T1 tumors (≤5 cm) but jump a full
stage to IIIA for T2 tumors (5 to 10 cm) and to IIIB for T3 and T4 tumors (>10 cm). This
indicates the importance of size as a prognostic factor.
Any regional or distant metastatic disease represents stage IV and supersedes any
primary tumor factors. Nodal disease is uncommon in soft-tissue sarcoma, with the
exception of rhabdomyosarcoma (separate staging system); epithelioid sarcoma; clear
cell sarcoma; and, less often, synovial sarcoma.

Rhabdomyosarcoma Staging
Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is unique because it is a small, round blue cell tumor with
metastatic patterns that differ from those of non-RMS soft-tissue sarcomas. Initial
staging systems used clinical groups based on the presence of metastatic disease, nodal
involvement, and residual disease postoperatively. Pre-management prognostic factors,
such as tumor size, primary site, histology (embryonal versus alveolar), and patient age,
were incorporated into TNM staging. Recently, the presence of gene fusions between
PAX and FOXO1 genes were found to convey an unfavorable prognosis, superseding
histologic type. Currently, fusion status is incorporated into risk stratification for staging,
which in turn determines treatment strategy (Resource 4).
The prognosis for children and young adults with non-RMS soft-tissue sarcoma is
affected by grade, tumor size, metastatic disease, and completeness of resection. In
general, this patient population can tolerate systemic chemotherapy better than adults;
however, the effects of radiation therapy in these patients may be worse (secondary
malignancy, growth arrest, fibrosis, etc.). Stratification of management based on known
risk factors is beneficial; this ensures that patients who require chemotherapy and
radiation therapy benefit from such treatment but avoids the associated risks of such
treatment in patients in whom it is not required. This is the current strategy for clinical
trials in the Children’s Oncology Group (Resource 5).
